trial_name: PROSEVA — Prone Positioning in Severe ARDS (2013)
citation: Guérin C, Reignier J, Richard JC et al. Prone positioning in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med 2013;368(23):2159–2168.
one_liner: In severe ARDS, early prolonged prone positioning reduced 28-day mortality from 32.8% to 16.0% (HR 0.39).

pico.population: Adults with severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg, FiO2 ≥0.60, PEEP ≥5 cm H2O) within 36 hours of invasive ventilation
pico.intervention: Early prolonged prone positioning sessions ≥16 hours/day, with lung-protective ventilation
pico.comparison: Supine (semi-recumbent) positioning with identical lung-protective ventilation

background.existing_knowledge: Prone positioning improves oxygenation in ARDS by redistributing transpulmonary pressures and ventilation–perfusion, reducing ventral overdistension and dorsal atelectrauma. Earlier RCTs in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure/ARDS improved oxygenation but did not consistently show a mortality benefit; many enrolled patients with less severe hypoxaemia and/or used shorter daily prone sessions, often before low tidal volume ventilation became standard.
background.knowledge_gap: It remained uncertain whether applying prone positioning early, for prolonged sessions, in a clearly defined severe ARDS population receiving lung-protective ventilation could deliver a survival benefit.
background.hypothesis: Early initiation of prolonged prone positioning sessions (≥16 consecutive hours/day) reduces 28-day mortality compared with supine positioning under a lung-protective ventilation strategy.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, investigator-initiated, open-label, parallel-group trial with central computer-generated allocation stratified by ICU (27 ICUs: 26 in France, 1 in Spain).
methods.setting: 27 ICUs (26 France, 1 Spain); enrollment period not specified.

inclusion: Adults with ARDS (acute onset, bilateral infiltrates, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg, no left atrial hypertension), intubated and invasively ventilated for <36 hours
Severe ARDS confirmed after 12–24 hour stabilisation: PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg, FiO2 ≥0.60, PEEP ≥5 cm H2O, tidal volume ~6 mL/kg predicted body weight
exclusion: Contraindication to prone positioning (e.g., unstable spine, raised ICP, recent tracheal surgery, massive haemoptysis)
Chronic respiratory failure requiring long-term oxygen or home NIV

methods.intervention: Prone positioning started as soon as possible after randomisation (mean 55 ± 55 minutes) and delivered in sessions of ≥16 consecutive hours (mean 17 ± 3 hours), repeated daily until pre-specified stopping criteria or day 28. Lung-protective ventilation in volume-controlled mode: tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight; plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O; PEEP/FiO2 table; permissive hypercapnia (target pH 7.20–7.45). Deep sedation targeted early; neuromuscular blockade strongly recommended during the first 48 hours and during prone sessions.
methods.comparison: Supine (semi-recumbent) positioning with identical protocolised lung-protective ventilation and supportive care. Crossover to prone positioning prohibited except as protocolised rescue for life-threatening hypoxaemia after optimisation and rescue measures (FiO2 1.0, maximal PEEP per table, inhaled nitric oxide 10 ppm, almitrine 4 µg/kg/min, recruitment manoeuvres).
methods.blinding: Unblinded (positioning not feasibly blindable); mortality objective, but co-interventions and liberation-from-ventilation decisions could be influenced by lack of blinding.
methods.sample_size_power: 456 patients required to detect a 15% absolute reduction in 28-day mortality (from 60% to 45%) with 90% power at a one-sided 5% significance level; interim analysis planned after 50% enrolment with two one-sided analyses at the 2.5% level.
secondary_outcomes: Successful extubation by day 90 (no reintubation or NIV within 48 hours)
Ventilator-free days at day 28 and day 90

headline_bullets: Successful extubation by day 90: 80.5% vs 65.0% (HR 0.45, P<0.001)
Ventilator-free days significantly higher in prone group (14 vs 10 at day 28, P<0.001)
Cardiac arrest less frequent in prone group (6.8% vs 13.5%, P=0.02); pneumothorax similar

outcomes_table.note: Defined as extubation without reintubation or NIV within 48 h
No CI reported for between-group comparison

safety: Pneumothorax: 6.3% prone vs 5.7% supine (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.39–2.02, P=0.85)
No other major safety concerns reported

domains.notes: Central computer-generated allocation stratified by ICU; web-based system supports allocation concealment.
474 randomised, 8 excluded post-randomisation for eligibility/procedural reasons, leaving 466 analysed (modified ITT). 90-day vital status reported for the analysed cohort.
Unblinded positioning could influence co-interventions and extubation decisions; primary endpoint (mortality) is objective and less vulnerable to ascertainment bias.
First prone session 55 ± 55 min after randomisation; mean 4 ± 4 sessions per patient; mean session duration 17 ± 3 h; prone positioning comprised 73% of total ICU hours in the prone group.
17/229 (7.4%) in supine group crossed to prone for refractory hypoxaemia per protocolised rescue; this direction biases estimates toward the null.

Severe ARDS severity well matched: PaO2/FiO2 100 ± 20 vs 100 ± 30; FiO2 0.74 ± 0.18 vs 0.74 ± 0.17; PEEP 10 ± 3 vs 10 ± 3 cm H2O; tidal volume 6.1 ± 0.6 vs 6.1 ± 0.6 mL/kg PBW. SAPS II 45 ± 15 vs 47 ± 17; SOFA 9.6 ± 3.2 vs 10.4 ± 3.4.

Randomisation after 12–24 h stabilisation and within 36 h of mechanical ventilation; time from intubation to randomisation 33 ± 24 h vs 31 ± 26 h. Sessions were long-duration (≥16 h; mean 17 h) and repeated.
High use of vasopressors (72.6% vs 83.0%) and neuromuscular blockers (91.0% vs 82.3%) at inclusion. Low use of inhaled nitric oxide (11.0% vs 14.4%), almitrine (3.8% vs 2.6%), ECMO (1.7% vs 2.2%).
Mortality endpoints analysed with Kaplan–Meier/log-rank and Cox regression stratified by centre; target sample size achieved (466 analysed vs 456 required). Large and consistent effect estimates.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears strong, supported by centralised stratified randomisation, objective primary outcome assessment, and excellent separation in prone “dose”; limitations include open-label care and small post-randomisation exclusions consistent with a modified intention-to-treat population.

domains.notes: Selected severe ARDS subset (466 analysed from 3,449 ARDS cases screened), with exclusions removing patients with common proning barriers (e.g., major contraindications, chronic respiratory failure).
Conducted in 27 ICUs (predominantly France) where all participating units reported routine prone positioning use for >5 years; may not reflect implementation conditions in less experienced ICUs.

Most applicable to invasively ventilated adults with severe ARDS receiving contemporary lung-protective ventilation, where a trained team can reliably deliver prolonged prone sessions and manage associated sedation, neuromuscular blockade, and line/airway risks.
Intervention is equipment-light but staff- and process-intensive; generalisability depends on staffing, training, and ability to maintain safety during turns and prolonged sessions.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate: PROSEVA provides high-confidence evidence for early prolonged proning in severe ARDS, but translation to milder ARDS, units without established proning expertise, or settings with limited staffing remains less certain.

strengths: Clear severe ARDS phenotype with protocolised stabilisation before randomisation
Early initiation and high “dose” of prone positioning with excellent protocol adherence (mean 17-hour sessions; repeated daily)
Contemporary lung-protective ventilation in both groups, supporting isolation of the positioning effect
Objective primary endpoint with consistent mortality benefit at day 28 and day 90
limitations: Open-label design introduces potential performance bias for co-interventions and weaning decisions
Highly experienced centres and selected population may limit real-world reproducibility without robust training and implementation programmes
Rescue crossover to prone in the control arm (7.4%) and co-intervention imbalances (e.g., neuromuscular blockade, vasopressors) complicate causal attribution in pragmatic deployment

critical_appraisal.summary: PROSEVA is a well-conducted, multicentre RCT with a large, consistent mortality benefit in severe ARDS. The open-label design and experienced centres require cautious generalisation, but the internal validity is strong.
strengths: Central stratified randomisation and objective primary endpoint minimise bias
Excellent protocol adherence with high-dose, early prone positioning
Use of contemporary lung-protective ventilation isolates the effect of positioning
weaknesses: Open-label design may affect co-interventions and extubation decisions
Eight post-randomisation exclusions require modified ITT analysis
Conducted in highly experienced ICUs, limiting generalisability to less prepared settings

sections.authors_conclusion: In severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg with high FiO2 and PEEP) managed with lung-protective ventilation, early prolonged prone positioning reduced 28-day mortality compared with supine management, with benefit persisting to day 90 and higher rates of successful extubation.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial changes practice: early, prolonged prone positioning should be standard for eligible patients with severe ARDS.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult patients with severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg, FiO2 ≥0.60, PEEP ≥5 cm H2O) within 36 hours of intubation, managed with lung-protective ventilation, in ICUs with experienced teams.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Proning is not a substitute for lung-protective ventilation; it is an adjunct. It is not indicated for mild ARDS or as a late rescue-only measure.
implementation_caveats: Requires trained staff and safety protocols for turning and managing lines/airway
Deep sedation and neuromuscular blockade may be needed, especially early
Early initiation (<36h of ventilation) is key
May not be feasible in all ICUs without prior expertise

controversies.notes: Editorial highlighted that PROSEVA was conducted in ICUs with substantial prior experience, raising implementation concerns about achieving similar outcomes in less experienced units.
The mortality effect size (HR 0.39) was larger than earlier proning trials, contextualised by differences in patient selection (more severe ARDS), earlier initiation, and longer daily prone exposure.
Published correspondence raised issues including interpretation of PaCO2 changes and logistics of CPR in the prone position, underscoring the need for safety protocols and team training.
Post-PROSEVA meta-analysis in the low tidal volume era confirmed reduced mortality with prone positioning, with benefit concentrated in more severe ARDS and with longer prone sessions.
International clinical practice guidelines after PROSEVA recommend prone positioning as a core therapy for moderate-to-severe/severe ARDS when deliverable safely by trained teams.

unresolved_questions: Effectiveness of prone positioning in ICUs without established expertise
Optimal duration and timing to stop prone sessions
Role of concurrent neuromuscular blockade in achieving benefit
Feasibility and safety of prone positioning during ECMO

numbers_to_remember: Mean prone session 17 h, 4 sessions, 73% of ICU time
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In severe ARDS, early prolonged prone positioning cuts mortality by half and should be implemented early with trained teams.
